title: Electric Field, Electric Flux and Gauss's Law
subcategory: Electric Charges and Fields — Field, Flux, Gauss's Law

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Electric Charges and Fields

summary: Electric field is force per unit test charge at a point; electric flux measures field lines passing through a surface, and Gauss's law relates the total flux through any closed surface to the charge it encloses — a powerful shortcut for symmetric charge distributions.
explanation: Electric field at a point is defined as E = F/q₀ (force per unit positive test charge, in the limit q₀ → 0 so the test charge doesn't disturb the source distribution), a vector field that can be visualised with field lines: they start on positive charges, end on negative charges, never cross, and their density indicates field strength. Electric flux through a surface, ΦE = ∮E·dA, measures the 'number' of field lines crossing that surface; it depends on the field, the surface area, and the angle between the field and the surface's normal. Gauss's law states ΦE (through any closed surface) = qenclosed/ε₀ — remarkably, this holds regardless of the size/shape of the closed (Gaussian) surface and regardless of charges OUTSIDE it (they contribute zero net flux). This is a general law (equivalent to Coulomb's law for static charges) but becomes an extremely efficient calculation shortcut when the charge distribution has high symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar) — letting you choose a Gaussian surface where E is uniform and either parallel or perpendicular everywhere. Applications: field due to an infinite line charge (E ∝ 1/r), an infinite plane sheet of charge (E is uniform, independent of distance from the sheet), and a uniformly charged spherical shell (E = 0 inside, behaves like a point charge at the centre for points outside). An electric dipole (two equal, opposite charges separated by a small distance) has a dipole moment p = q×2a (from −q to +q); its field falls off faster (∝1/r³ on the axial/equatorial line) than a single point charge's field (∝1/r²), and in a uniform external field, a dipole experiences zero net force but a torque τ = p×E that tends to align it with the field.
commonMisconceptions: Believing Gauss's law only applies to symmetric charge distributions — it is universally true for ANY closed surface and ANY charge distribution; it is just most USEFUL for calculation when symmetry lets you simplify the flux integral.

Assuming charges outside the Gaussian surface don't affect the electric field at points on the surface — they still contribute to the field (and can affect its direction/uniformity), they simply contribute zero NET flux through the closed surface.
Treating field lines as real physical lines with mass or existence rather than a visualisation tool that always follows the rule 'no two field lines cross.'
examples: Inside a uniformly charged hollow spherical shell, the electric field is exactly zero everywhere, regardless of how the charge is distributed on the shell (as long as it's uniform/symmetric).
The field near an infinite charged plane sheet is the same at 1 cm or 1 km away, unlike a point charge's field which weakens with distance.
genZNote: Gauss's law: forget every charge outside the surface — this closed surface only cares about what's inside.
